To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the discovery of vaccine candidates has been greatly accelerated in the post‐genomic age, and that we now have a plethora of vaccine candidates that are ready for testing, but that we still lack the tools and the models to determine their efficacy in a cost‐efficient way.
although we have significantly expanded our repertoire of potential vaccine candidates for malaria, a bottleneck in their prioritization for evaluation remains.

Although we have exponentially increased the number of potential vaccine candidates identified in a relatively short time, a significant bottle neck still exists in their validation and priority for evaluation in clinical trial.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and validation of new technologies for the discovery and characterization of novel vaccine candidates for Plasmodia falciparum.
the identification of novel malaria vaccine candidates and the development of new technologies for the rapid evaluation of these vaccine candidates.
understanding how the immune system responds to the presence of malaria parasites, and the mechanisms that underlie protective immunity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
although the number of potential vaccine targets has increased exponentially, the number of validated candidates has not.
although we are better equipped than ever to identify numerous potential malaria vaccine candidates, the bottleneck remains in their evaluation.
the discovery of vaccine candidates has been successful, but the identification of a vaccine has not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the next generation of subunit vaccines will likely require the integration of several of the methodologies described herein.

the next generation of subunit malaria vaccines should include multiple antigens, be formulated in a manner that induces a broad range of protective antibody functions and be administered to individuals at high risk of infection in endemic settings.
we are not yet in the position to predict which of the many potential vaccine candidates are likely to be the most effective in inducing protection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to continue to identify new vaccine candidates and test them in human trials to find the best combination that provides protection.

the next generation of vaccines for the prevention and treatment of malaria will require the identification and characterization of a small number of highly effective antigens that are able to induce potent and long‐lasting immune responses.
we need to be more critical of our vaccine discovery efforts.
